stem: A financial institution aims to develop a model for detecting fraudulent credit card transactions. It possesses a history of transaction data in which instances of fraud and non-fraud are clearly labeled and explicitly identified. What is the appropriate machine learning technique the financial institution should adopt?

options.A: Supervised.
options.B: Unsupervised.
options.C: Reinforcement.
options.D: Semi-supervised.

rationale: The correct answer is A. In this situation, where the financial institution has a labeled dataset with instances of fraud and non-fraud clearly identified, the appropriate machine learning technique is supervised learning. In supervised learning, the model is trained on labeled data, and it learns to make predictions or classifications based on the provided labels. The goal is to identify patterns in the labeled data that can be used to accurately predict the labels for new, unseen instances . Body of Knowledge Domain I, Competency A

stem: Supermarket Limited is a global supermarket chain and is rapidly introducing AI systems into its business to drive efficiency and quality. Its human resources, marketing and quality control departments are the priority. Supermarket Limited's AI Officer is putting together a cross-functional team of lawyers to help advise on the AI aspects of these projects, but due to budgetary constraints the team can only consist of three lawyers. Which of the following disciplines would be most appropriate for the AI Officer to focus on?

options.A: Employment, patents, anti-trust.
options.B: Litigation, healthcare, product safety.
options.C: Copyright, data protection, employment.
options.D: Product safety, contracts, government relations.

rationale: The correct answer is C. Copyright will be relevant to generative AI systems used to create marketing materials, while data protection and employment expertise will be relevant to AI systems used for recruitment and allocating job responsibilities. While product safety expertise would also be very helpful for AI systems relating to the quality control, the other legal disciplines mentioned (contracts, government relations, patents, litigation and anti-trust) are less relevant to the stated goals of Supermarket Limited and interaction with AI laws. Body of Knowledge Domain IV, Competency B

scenarioText: Amy is a data scientist who works for a health care company in France. She is asked to develop a plan to build a machine learning model that predicts patient satisfaction with doctors based on an analysis of the doctors' notes. The doctors are from various countries , and the notes are in free-form text, compiled in a database in Germany.
stem: Which of the following is the best answer for what Amy's first step should be?

options.A: Clean the data to remove any outliers and missing values.
options.B: Perform a data lineage analysis to determine where the data originated.
options.C: Start building a predictive model that can be used to assess client satisfaction.
options.D: Examine the data for unexpected insights, concepts and semantic relationships.

rationale: The correct answer is B. Given the strong privacy and data protection laws in this region, privacy and data transfer laws must be considered first. EU, French and German laws must be reviewed before any other activity is performed. This is achieved by reviewing where the data originates, where it is transferred and what laws control this path, as well as the use of the data. While removing outliers and missing items; or examining insights, concepts and semantics are vital aspects of the AI development process, laws may disallow the processing or movement of the data entirely. In addition, building the model to the client's satisfaction occurs further along in the AI development process and is ill-advised. Body of Knowledge Domain III, Competency B

scenarioText: Amy is a data scientist who works for a health care company in France. She is asked to develop a plan to build a machine learning model that predicts patient satisfaction with doctors based on an analysis of the doctors' notes. The doctors are from various countries , and the notes are in free-form text, compiled in a database in Germany.
stem: Assuming Amy has complied with all privacy and data protection laws, what type of machine learning is Amy most likely to use to predict patient satisfaction?

options.A: Regression.
options.B: Decision tree.
options.C: Dimensionality reduction.
options.D: Natural language processing.

rationale: The correct answer is D. Since the doctors' notes are in free-form text, natural language processing would be the most likely type of machine learning used. NLP is specifically used for analyzing text and natural language. Regression is used typically for predicting numerical values where there are underlying variables that are numeric. A decision tree is used typically for classification where a limited number of variables are involved. Dimensionality reduction is used to reduce the number of variables and other extraneous factors, so is not likely to be used, given the other options. Body of Knowledge Domain IV, Competency A

stem: When initiating an AI governance program, which of the following statements best reflects a strategic approach to effectively engaging leadership?

options.A: Identify leaders already using AI who see opportunities for differentiation through improved governance.
options.B: Postpone leadership engagement until the AI program is fully implemented to avoid an overly complicated journey.
options.C: Prioritize leaders with extensive business experience to help minimize discussions about responsible AI and simplify your decision-making process.
options.D: Get buy-in from leaders whose primary interest centers around the ability of AI to allow the organization to get ahead of its competition.

rationale: The correct answer is A. In the context of AI governance, it is crucial to engage leaders who not only have experience with AI, but also recognize the potential for differentiation through responsible practices. This approach ensures leadership alignment with the AI governance program goals and helps in understanding the value it brings. Body of Knowledge Domain I, Competency B

stem: The EU AI Act and NIST AI Risk Management Framework are both pursuing the dual purposes of promoting the uptake of AI and addressing the risks associated with its use. Which of the following is one of themain differences between the EU AI Act and NIST AI RMF?

options.A: The EU AI Act is underpinned by a risk-based approach, while the NIST AI RMF is a horizontal regulation.
options.B: The EU AI Act is applicable to EU-based companies only, while the NIST AI RMF has an extraterritorial effect.
options.C: The EU AI Act is relevant to large- and medium-sized companies, while NIST AI RMF applies to companies of all sizes.
options.D: The EU AI Act imposes mandatory compliance requirements, while NIST AI RMF is a voluntary AI governance framework.

rationale: The correct answer is D. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework is intended for voluntary use and to improve the ability to incorporate trustworthiness considerations into the design, development, use and evaluation of AI products, services and systems. The EU AI Act imposes comprehensive mandatory compliance requirements on high-risk AI with respect to, among other things, risk mitigation, data governance, detailed documentation, human oversight, transparency, robustness, accuracy and cybersecurity. The EU AI Act requires mandatory conformity assessments and fundamental rights impact assessments .It also provides a right for citizens to launch complaints about AI systems and receive explanations about decisions based on high-risk AI systems that impact their rights. Body of Knowledge Domain II, Competency C

stem: Robotic processing automation is an emerging type of artificial intelligence. Which of the following does NOT describe RPA?

options.A: Machines that mimic human actions on digital systems.
options.B: Software robots that are used to automate rule-based tasks.
options.C: Machines designed to perform tasks relying on human intervention.
options.D: Software robots that are augmented by other types of artificial intelligence.

rationale: The correct answer is C. The intent of robotic processing automation is to “mimic” human behavior by leveraging intelligent systems. The goal of this is to decrease human intervention by automating tasks to increase efficiency of business processes, and not rely on humans to complete tasks. Body of Knowledge Domain I, Competency A

stem: A retailer plans to implement facial recognition in physical stores. Which of the following measures should the retailer take to comply with regulatory requirements?

options.A: Disclose the practice of facial recognition to consumers.
options.B: Train the employees not to reveal the use of facial recognition technology.
options.C: Ensure as many images as possible are placed into the facial-matching system.
options.D: Consult with a trusted privacy professional network to source a facial-recognition vendor.

rationale: The correct answer is A. Transparency is a key value in privacy and responsible AI. Failure to disclose risks of harm to consumers can also lead to violations of the FTC Act section 5, as well as existing privacy laws such as the GDPR, and potentially to violations of emerging laws. Companies that use facial recognition in physical stores should, at a minimum, consider disclosing the practice to consumers. Body of Knowledge Domain III, Competency C

stem: Company N works in the field of disability benefits and wants to use AI to determine who is most likely to benefit from its services by filtering applications. Company N's privacy officer is concerned about unintended serious impacts of filtering applications. What is a negative impact the privacy officer should consider when analyzing the proposed project?

options.A: Impacting an employee's job.
options.B: Making individuals uncomfortable.
options.C: Discriminating against a particular group.
options.D: Creating a false sense of security for applicants.

rationale: The correct answer is C. The privacy officer should examine the project carefully to determine if there will be an unintended result of discrimination against a particular group of individuals who may share a trait that will accidentally cause the AI to filter out their applications for disability benefits, even though they would normally qualify. Body of Knowledge Domain I, Competency A

stem: Which of the following is NOT a key component of AI governance policies to ensure oversight and accountability across all AI lifecycle stages?

options.A: Implementing a data privacy compliance program.
options.B: Establishing a centralized AI governance committee.
options.C: Promoting a culture of innovation and experimentation.
options.D: Developing comprehensive AI risk assessment frameworks.

rationale: The correct answer is C. While innovation and experimentation are essential for AI development, they should be balanced with robust governance to ensure ethical and responsible AI practices. The other options (A, B and C) are all critical components of AI governance , as they provide oversight, risk management and compliance. A culture of innovation without proper governance can lead to unintended consequences, such as biased models or privacy breaches. Body of Knowledge Domain I, Competency C

stem: Kim is expanding their governance, risk and compliance role at their organization to include the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. Kim is using the four core functions to lay out their project to present to management. Which of the following is the step for the measure function?

options.A: Risk management is cultivated and present.
options.B: Identified risks are assessed, analyzed or tracked.
options.C: Risk is prioritized and acted upon based on projected impact.
options.D: Context is recognized and risks related to context are identified.

rationale: The correct answer is B. The measure function involves quantifying risks and their related impacts, including tracking trustworthiness and social impacts. Through this stage, organizations can balance any trade-offs necessary and ensure the risks are mitigated where possible. Body of Knowledge Domain II, Competency D

stem: An organization is in the process of integrating an open-source AI model into its operations and needs to evaluate the vendor agreement. Which of the following considerations is most critical for ensuring that the organization understands potential risks and obligations related to data privacy and intellectual property?

options.A: Evaluate the compliance of the AI model with existing organizational policies to ensure consistency with internal practices and procedures.
options.B: Review the license type of the open-source AI model to ensure it aligns with the organization's commercial goals and does not impose restrictions on distribution.
options.C: Examine the terms regarding the model's training data, including ownership, usage rights and any obligations for sharing derivative works based on the open-source model.
options.D: Assess whether the agreement includes clauses for liability limitations, as these can impact the organization's recourse in the event of a data breach or model malfunction. For the next question ONLY:Selectallthat applies.

rationale: The correct answer is C. Understanding the terms regarding the model's training data is essential for assessing data privacy risks, potential intellectual property issues, and compliance with data protection regulations. Ownership and usage rights of training data can significantly impact the organization's obligations and rights, especially in relation to user data and the use of derivative works from the model. While reviewing the license type is important, it focuses more on distribution and commercial goals rather than the immediate risks associated with data privacy and intellectual property, which are paramount when integrating an AI model that handles sensitive data. Liability limitations are also important, but this option does not directly address the critical elements of data usage and ownership, which are vital for privacy compliance and the ethical use of AI. And while alignment with internal policies is beneficial, it does not address the external risks tied to data privacy and intellectual property outlined in the vendor or open- source agreement. By focusing on C, organizations can better safeguard their interests and comply with relevant laws and regulations when leveraging open-source AI technologies. Body of Knowledge Domain IV Competency B

stem: Which of the following outline some of the necessary components of creating an AI governance structure?

options.A: Identify an executive champion
options.B: Identify applicable laws
options.C: Determine whether there is an AI governance structure
options.D: Identify and document who will implement AI governance structure
options.E: Establish and document data lineage This is amulti-select question.There is more than one correct option. You must selectALLthe correct options to earn one point on the Answer Key tally. The Answer Sheet has been left blank to allow you to enter your selections.

rationale: The correct answer is A, C and D. While identifying laws and establishing data lineage are important stages of AI implementation, they are not part of creating the governance structure. Typically, one would first determine whether an AI governance structure is already in place; then, if not, or if a new structure is needed, decide who the executive champion is and determine who will maintain the structure. Body of Knowledge Domain I, Competency B

stem: Which of the following is a key component of the NIST ARIA program for AI safety?

options.A: AI Ethics Guidelines.
options.B: AI Governance Framework.
options.C: AI Safety Assurance Framework.
options.D: AI Risk Assessment Framework.

rationale: The correct answer is D. The NIST ARIA program (Artificial Intelligence Risk Assessment) is primarily focused on assessing and managing risks associated with AI systems. The AI Risk Assessment Framework is a central component of this program, providing a structured approach to identifying , assessing and mitigating risks. While the other options (AI Safety Assurance Framework, AI Ethics Guidelines and AI Governance Framework) are also important aspects of AI safety, they are not the central focus of the NIST ARIA program. Body of Knowledge Domain II, Competency D

stem: What is the purpose of a risk assessment in AI Governance?

options.A: Test and validate the AI system.
options.B: Establish priorities and allocate resources.
options.C: Compile feedback from impacted AI actors.
options.D: Establish appropriate roles and responsibilities.

rationale: The correct answer is B. The purpose of a risk assessment is to identify the areas of greatest risk in an AI system so risk mitigation resources can be allocated appropriately. Risk assessments can also be used to generate metrics for tracking and managing priorities throughout the model development life cycle. Body of Knowledge Domain III, Competency A

stem: An India-based company has developed an AI system to assist recruiters for initial screening of resumes based on certain criteria, which can also be modified as per customer's needs. When considering expanding to the EU market, this type of technology would?

options.A: Require the company to register the tool with the EU database.
options.B: Require the company to get approval by the relevant EU authority.
options.C: Require the company to perform a detailed conformity assessment.
options.D: Require the company to appoint an EU representative to handle queries from the EU market.

rationale: The correct answer is C. Under the EU AI Act, high-risk AI systems (like systems dealing with recruitment) would require a detailed conformity assessment before being deployed in the EU market. This assessment ensures that the AI system complies with all relevant regulations and standards, addressing potential risks related to privacy, security and discrimination. Body of Knowledge Domain IV, Competency B

stem: John is the AI governance lead for his EU-based company, XYZ. XYZ provides users with a virtual assistant. When exiting the system, users receive a notice which informs them they have interacted with an AI system and its responses may include hallucinations that should be reviewed by the user. John informs XYZ of his approval of this notice along with the way it is presented to him. Based on the information provided, why is XYZ not in compliance with the transparency requirements set out by the EU AI Act?

options.A: The notice is not GDPR compliant.
options.B: The notice was not displayed in a timely manner.
options.C: The notice is not accessible to vulnerable persons.
options.D: The notice is not adequate in terms of the information provided.

rationale: The correct answer is B. As per the transparency obligations set forth in the EU AI Act, the notice that informs users they are using an AI system shall be provided, at the latest, at the time of first interaction or exposure to the AI system in question. In this case, the notice was provided as a response to the first prompt rather than being displayed to users at the time of the first interaction or exposure, before they enter a prompt. Body of Knowledge Domain II, Competency C

stem: Which of the following is a critical term to assess in an open-source AI vendor agreement regarding the use of the software?

options.A: Data Ownership.
options.B: Marketing Rights.
options.C: Termination Clause.
options.D: Non-Disclosure Agreement.

rationale: The correct answer is A. Since the vendor is open source, it is critical to address clauses related to data ownership, to ensure no copyrighted data is being used without consent which could lead to infringement claims. Additionally, specifying in the agreement who ultimately owns the output will determine who has the right to use it and how it can be used. Body of Knowledge Domain IV, Competency B

stem: DPIAs and AI conformity assessments are both important tools in evaluating privacy risk. Which of the following is a key component of both?

options.A: A targeted mitigation plan.
options.B: An effective consent model.
options.C: A strategy to anonymize data.
options.D: A policy for personal data use.

rationale: The correct answer is A. Both assessments should involve an assessment of risks, as well as a plan to mitigate such risks. Consent and anonymization may be needed depending on the process or system involved. While personal data is a component of a DPIA , it may or may not be for an AI conformity assessment. Body of Knowledge Domain II, Competency C

stem: How can human oversight influence the reduction of bias or discrimination in AI/ML models (algorithmic bias) in the initial stages of selecting data and defining goals?

options.A: Using only data scientists to handle data selection in AI/ML models ensures success in meeting set goals.
options.B: Working with a variety of social experts ensures inclusive and unbiased data during the AI/ML model design.
options.C: Having software engineers manage AI/ML bias reduction without social science input provides clarity in data selection.
options.D: Allowing government regulators to provide the sole definition of AI/ML model data will remove all bias and discrimination.

rationale: The correct answer is B. Collaboration with social experts, such as psychologists, linguists and sociologists, provides diverse insights into human behavior and societal dynamics essential for identifying potential biases that may not be obvious to data scientists or software engineers. Body of Knowledge Domain III, Competency A

stem: What is the purpose of liability reform regarding liability for AI systems?

options.A: To discourage the development and adoption of AI systems.
options.B: To increase the legal risks and costs associated with AI systems.
options.C: To reduce the legal certainty for developers and users of AI systems.
options.D: To change the governing rules accountability for damages caused by AI systems.

rationale: The correct answer is D. Liability reform is the process of changing the legal rules and principles that govern the responsibility and accountability of parties who cause or contribute to damage or harm through AI systems. Body of Knowledge Domain II, Competency B

stem: When building an AI model, which of the following is a best practice for feature selection?

options.A: Raw data is preferred to processed data.
options.B: The more features used, the better the model performs.
options.C: Personal information should never be used as a feature.
options.D: The same features must be used for training and testing.

rationale: The correct answer is D. Training and testing data must use the same features to ensure accuracy. There are trade-offs to adding model features in performance, and adding too many features can cause overfitting to the training data. Raw data needs to be processed before being added to the model, at the very least, for data cleaning purposes. Finally, personal information can be used as a feature, but only where necessary. Body of Knowledge Domain III, Competency B

stem: Company XBR is developing an AI system for a virtual assistant to be used in households. How would the development team incorporate the principles of human-centric design throughout the entire process, from conception to deployment?

options.A: Ignoring privacy concerns to maximize data collection for refining the AI algorithms.
options.B: Designing the virtual assistant to operate independently, without requiring user input.
options.C: Prioritizing user feedback and involving potential users in the early stages of development.
options.D: Focusing on technical advancements and automation to streamline the virtual assistant's capabilities.

rationale: The correct answer is C. The development team should rely on users' participation and feedback to incorporate the principles of human-centric design through the process, from development to deployment of the AI system. Human-centered AI learns from human input and collaboration, and continuously improves based on human feedback. Prioritizing users' feedback and involving users in the development of the AI system or otherwise is known as “human-centered design,” which is an approach to interactive systems development that aims to make systems usable and useful by focusing on the users, and their needs and requirements, and by applying human factors/ ergonomics, usability knowledge and techniques. This approach enhances effectiveness and efficiency, improves human well-being, user satisfaction, accessibility and sustainability; and counteracts possible adverse effects of use on human health, safety and performance. See ISO 9241-210:2019(E) Body of Knowledge Domain I, Competency A

stem: Which one of the following options contains elements that should be considered when building an AI incident response plan?

options.A: The security incident plan, which covers all requirements needed, includes required incident actions so the security team can oversee AI incident management.
options.B: The third-party tools that are integrated into your system should be identified because, in the case of an incident, you might need to notify those third parties.
options.C: An automated tool should be in place to guarantee the algorithm is shut down immediately, avoiding dependence on human action to avoid delays or human error.
options.D: The existing privacy breach response tools in your organization need to be reused, as the data privacy team should be the reporting body overseeing all data-related incidents.

rationale: The correct answer is B. To understand third-party risk in the organization, it is necessary to identify all third- party tools that are integrated in the system. If there is an incident, the organization might need to notify the user of these third-party tools, as the incident might not only impact the tool owned by the organization. Body of Knowledge Domain I, Competency C

stem: The HR department of the EU-based CompanyX purchases an AI-enabled tool to optimize efficiency and resource allocation. The tool collects personal data, including special categories of personal data under the GDPR, for an automated rating of workers' performance and assignment of work. Given the context, the tool might be qualified as a high-risk AI system under the EU AI Act. Consequently, CompanyX must conduct tests against preliminarily defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds to identify risks and the most appropriate risk management measures. Since the tool will be used for automated decision-making affecting the privacy rights of employees, CompanyX must?

options.A: Carry out a conformity assessment procedure after working with a representative in the EU.
options.B: Draft the technical documentation and the required instructions for use once the tool is ready for use.
options.C: Perform a data protection impact assessment to determine the impact to personal data before launching the tool.
options.D: Inform appropriate national authorities of the Member States of all the risk mitigations taken as soon as the tool is in use.

rationale: The correct answer is C. CompanyX is an EU-based AI user and, therefore, it will need to comply with the requirements of the EU AI Act. The EU AI Act classifies AI systems used in employment and worker management as high risk and imposes rigorous obligations on the providers of high-risk AI systems. Users of high-risk AI tools must comply with less stringent requirements, such as using the product according to provider instructions; conducting impact assessments, including data protection impact assessments; monitoring the operation of the system; and informing the provider or distributor of system malfunctions. Carrying out a data protection impact assessment in this context is a GDPR requirement since the type of processing activity described creates a likelihood of a high-risk outcome to the rights and freedoms of the employees. Body of Knowledge Domain II, Competency C

scenarioText: ABC Corp. has purchased a software tool from Phlunk, Inc. that will analyze application logs for threats in their network. ABC has over 1 million log patterns that it has manually labeled as either “threat” and “non-threat.” ABC has trained a model extensively in their development environment with very strong F1 scores. After deploying their model into their production environment to classify incoming log patterns as threats or non- threats, they have found it generates too many false positives, drowning their security team in wasted effort. It has also been found that the model is generating false negatives , ie, not finding threats.
stem: Which of the following best describes why ABC Corp. had these issues?

options.A: The model suffers from concept drift.
options.B: Their training data was improperly labeled.
options.C: They did not properly test Phlunk's software tool.
options.D: They did not have a model inference process in place.

rationale: The correct answer is D. ABC has no procedure in place to test the accuracy of the model after it's deployed. Any deployed model must have a separate process for testing a model's performance in the real world, that is, in production. This is a failure of a basic machine learning governance stage called “inference.” Concept and improperly-labeled data would be reflected in model accuracy, which the facts state is not an issue. Since the model has been extensively trained, it is not a testing issue. Body of Knowledge Domain III, Competency C

scenarioText: ABC Corp. has purchased a software tool from Phlunk, Inc. that will analyze application logs for threats in their network. ABC has over 1 million log patterns that it has manually labeled as either “threat” and “non-threat.” ABC has trained a model extensively in their development environment with very strong F1 scores. After deploying their model into their production environment to classify incoming log patterns as threats or non- threats, they have found it generates too many false positives, drowning their security team in wasted effort. It has also been found that the model is generating false negatives , ie, not finding threats.
stem: To mitigate the false negatives issue, ABC Corp. has decided it wants to increase the accuracy of its model to account for potentially unknown threats. Which of the following approaches is the best solution?

options.A: Synthetic data.
options.B: Data minimization.
options.C: Federated learning.
options.D: Probabilistic graphical models.

rationale: The correct answer is A. Synthetic data is specifically used to increase the accuracy of models. Using agentbased modeling, this process generates possible new threats that mimic real data. Effective AI requires a significant amount of data, so data minimization is not a good solution. Federated learning is a technique used to assist with training on private or sensitive data in a way that is compliant with privacy laws. It has nothing to do with finding unknown threats. Probabilistic graphical models are used to represent dependencies and correlations between features . It has no applicability in this context. Body of Knowledge, Domain III, Competency C

stem: Which of the following is a crucial aspect of a deactivation policy for AI models?

options.A: The ability to immediately shut down a model if it generates profits.
options.B: Ensuring that only technical staff are aware of the deactivation process.
options.C: The capacity to disable the model due to legal or performance concerns.
options.D: Disabling the former AI model fully whenever a new model version is released.

rationale: The correct answer is C. A deactivation policy ensures that an AI model can be safely and effectively shut down if it no longer complies with regulatory requirements or exhibits significant performance issues, thus reducing risks to users and stakeholders. However, disabling a model due to profits is clearly not in the company's best interest; and new versions of the same product should not require fully disabling the model since new versions should build upon the prior one and would therefore use the same or a similar model. Body of Knowledge Domain IV, Competency C

stem: An organization wants to build a model to analyze content on social media by considering both textual content and associated images or videos. Which type of machine learning modeling technique is suitable in this scenario?

options.A: Regression.
options.B: Multi-modal.
options.C: Reinforcement.
options.D: Anomaly detection.

rationale: The correct answer is B. Multi-modal models are designed to process and integrate information from multiple modalities, making them well suited for tasks that involve diverse types of data, such as text, images and videos. In the given scenario, where the organization wants to analyze content on social media by developing a model that processes both textual content and associated images or videos, the resulting model would be regarded as multi-modal. Body of Knowledge Domain IV, Competency A

stem: The engineering team within your company has been working on an AI tool for the past several months. After completion of planning, design and development, what is the next step?

options.A: Perform a readiness assessment.
options.B: Define the business requirements.
options.C: Determine the governance structure.
options.D: Verify the data used to test the system.

rationale: The correct answer is A. Although the other options reference some part of the AI development life cycle, these steps should be completed before commencement of the implementation phase and during system planning, design and development. After the completion of these activities, a readiness assessment will determine whether the technology is ready to deploy. Body of Knowledge Domain III, Competency C

stem: Which of the following activities is a best practice method to identify and mitigate predictable risks of secondary or unintended uses of AI models?

options.A: Developing model cards for AI systems.
options.B: Implementing an AI governance strategy.
options.C: Conducting data protection impact assessments.
options.D: Engaging in bug bashing and red teaming exercises.

rationale: The correct answer is A. Model cards are short summary documents explaining the purpose of an AI model and provide information regarding a model's development and performance, as well as additional details for model transparency purposes. These cards are considered as a best practice method to identify and mitigate predictable risks associated with any secondary/unintended AI model use. Body of Knowledge Domain III, Competency C

stem: Which strategies are crucial for upskilling and reskilling the workforce to leverage AI benefits? (Choose Three)

options.A: Offering advanced AI courses only to IT professionals
options.B: Implementing company-wide training programs
options.C: Establishing partnerships with educational institutions
options.D: Providing incentives for self-learning

rationale: Comprehensive, company-wide training, partnerships with educational institutions, and incentives for self-learning all help a workforce responsibly leverage AI benefits. Restricting training to IT staff or ignoring existing skills works against workforce readiness.

stem: Mapping, planning, and scoping an AI project should ideally result in what?

options.A: Unclear project directives
options.B: Defined roles and responsibilities
options.C: Increased project costs
options.D: Extended project timelines

rationale: A proper mapping, planning and scoping exercise produces defined roles and responsibilities for the AI project, which is the foundation for accountable governance.

stem: Identify the major aspects of the OECD framework for classifying AI systems. (Choose Three)

options.A: Technology used
options.B: Level of automation
options.C: Role of humans
options.D: Environmental impact

rationale: The OECD classification framework centers on the technology used, the level of automation, and the output of the system (along with the role of humans and data/input, per the fuller five-dimension model). Environmental impact is not one of its core classification aspects.

stem: How can companies remain productive while using automated checks for AI governance?

options.A: By frequently updating their compliance protocols
options.B: Ignoring evolving standards
options.C: Avoiding automation in governance checks
options.D: Sticking to outdated technologies

rationale: Automated governance checks stay useful only if compliance protocols are updated frequently to track evolving standards and technology.

stem: Under what conditions can innovative AI be tested according to the EU AI Act, without standard compliance?

options.A: In any condition if profitability is demonstrated.
options.B: Never; all AI must comply without exemptions.
options.C: When specific exemptions for research apply.
options.D: Only if the AI is used by government entities.

rationale: The EU AI Act allows testing of innovative AI outside standard compliance only where specific research exemptions and regulatory sandbox procedures apply.

stem: Identify the key components of the AI technology stack. (Choose Two)

options.A: Platforms and applications
options.B: Chemical engineering techniques
options.C: Model types
options.D: Sports analytics

rationale: The AI technology stack includes platforms/applications and model types, alongside compute infrastructure (hardware and software). Chemical engineering and sports analytics are unrelated fields.

stem: Ensuring interoperability of AI risk management with other operational risk strategies involves what?

options.A: Overlooking other risk management frameworks
options.B: Integrating AI risk considerations into the broader risk management plan
options.C: Focusing only on AI-specific risks
options.D: Eliminating traditional risk management strategies

rationale: Interoperability means folding AI risk considerations into the organization’s broader enterprise risk management plan rather than treating AI risk in isolation.

stem: Which are types of machine learning training methods? (Choose Two)

options.A: Supervised
options.B: Unsupervised
options.C: Inductive
options.D: Reinforcement

rationale: Supervised and unsupervised learning are standard ML training methods (along with semi-supervised and reinforcement learning). "Inductive" is not one of the recognized training-method categories in the AIGP body of knowledge.

stem: According to the EU AI Act, which type of AI system is subject to the strictest regulations?

options.A: High-risk
options.B: Limited risk
options.C: Low risk
options.D: Prohibited

rationale: Prohibited AI practices face the strictest treatment under the EU AI Act: they are banned outright, which is stricter than the compliance obligations placed on high-risk systems.

stem: Identify a characteristic of an AI system that supports democratic processes effectively.

options.A: Enhancing public trust and transparency.
options.B: Prioritizing automation over human judgment.
options.C: Maximizing AI system opacity.
options.D: Focusing on profitability over ethics.

rationale: Systems that enhance public trust and transparency support democratic processes; opacity, profit-first design, and displacing human judgment undermine them.

stem: Machine learning is best described as a type of algorithm by which?

options.A: Systems can mimic human intelligence with the goal of performing routine tasks.
options.B: Systems can automatically improve from experience through predictive patterns.
options.C: Statistical inferences are drawn from a sample with the goal of predicting human intelligence.
options.D: Previously unknown properties are discovered in data and used to predict and make improvements in the data.

rationale: Why B is correct: Machine Learning (ML) is a subset of Artificial Intelligence in which systems learn from data without being explicitly programmed for each individual task. The key concept is that the system "automatically improves through experience", identifying predictive patterns in the data. Difference from the other options: • A describes AI in the broad sense (mimicking human intelligence), not specifically ML. • C describes classical statistical inference, which is a tool of ML but not its definition. • D describes data mining / unsupervised learning in a more specific sense, not ML in its entirety. Key concept to remember: ML ≠ AI (ML is a subset of AI). The characteristic that distinguishes it is experience-based self-improvement (experience-based improvement) through predictive patterns, without explicit reprogramming. Source: AIGP Study Supplement (Captain Compliance, v2.0) — Domain I, Competency I.A: "Machine learning (ML) is a subfield of AI concerned with the development of algorithms that enable computers to learn from data without being explicitly programmed."

topic: Types of ML Models — Random Forest
stem: Random forest algorithms are in what type of machine learning model?

options.A: Symbolic.
options.B: Generative.
options.C: Discriminative.
options.D: Natural language processing.

rationale: Why C is correct: Discriminative models learn to distinguish between classes or categories of data — in practice, they classify an input as belonging to one category rather than another. Random Forest is an ensemble of decision trees that classifies data into categories: it is therefore discriminative by definition. Key distinction to remember for the exam: • Discriminative Models → classify / distinguish existing data. Examples: Random Forest, Support Vector Machine (SVM), logistic regression. • Generative Models → create new data that "resembles" the training data. Examples: GPT, DALL·E, GAN (Generative Adversarial Networks). Why the others are wrong: • A (Symbolic) refers to systems based on rules and symbolic logic (e.g., expert systems), not to statistical ML. • B (Generative) refers to models that generate new content — Random Forest does not generate data, it classifies. • D (NLP) is an application/domain, not a type of ML model. Source: AIGP Study Supplement — "Discriminative models classify data into categories. Examples include decision trees and Random Forests."

stem: A company developed AI technology that can analyze text, video, images and sound to tag content, including the names of animals, humans and objects. What type of AI is this technology classified as?

options.A: Deductive inference.
options.B: Multi-modal model.
options.C: Transformative AI.
options.D: Expert system.

rationale: Why B is correct: A multi-modal model is a type of AI system designed to process and understand information coming from several sensory or input modalities simultaneously. In the case described, the system analyzes text, video, images and sound at the same time — this is exactly the definition of multi-modal. Key characteristics of multi-modal models: • They process multiple types of data in an integrated way (text + images + audio + video). • They can answer questions about images in natural language. • Practical examples: GPT-4o, Gemini, OpenAI's CLIP. • Advantage: a richer, more "human" understanding of information. Why the others are wrong: • A (Deductive inference) is a logical reasoning process, not a type of AI system. • C (Transformative AI) is not an official category recognized in the AIGP/IAPP vocabulary. • D (Expert system) is a system based on explicit rules defined by human experts — it does not learn from data. Source: AIGP Study Supplement — Domain I, Competency I.B: "Multi-modal models are a type of AI system that can process and understand information from multiple modalities, such as images, text, and audio."

stem: If it is possible to provide a rationale for a specific output of an AI system, that system can best be described as:

options.A: Accountable.
options.B: Transparent.
options.C: Explainable.
options.D: Reliable.

rationale: Why C is correct: Explainability is the ability of an AI system to provide an understandable justification for a specific output — that is, "why the system made this decision". This property is distinct from Transparency. Critical distinction on the exam (very frequent!): • Explainability = the ability to explain the REASON for a specific output. E.g.: "The loan was denied because your income is below the required minimum and you have a history of late payments." • Transparency = the ability to understand HOW the system works in general (structure, data used, algorithms). E.g.: "This system uses a Random Forest with 500 trees trained on data from the last 5 years." • Accountability = who answers for the consequences of the system's decisions. • Reliability = the system produces consistent and dependable results over time. Why Explainability is fundamental for AI governance: It enables people affected by automated decisions to understand and challenge those decisions. The GDPR (Arts. 13-15 and 22) explicitly provides for the right to "meaningful information about the logic" of automated systems. Source: AIGP Study Guide (Peter H. Gregory) — "Explainability is the characteristic of an AI system that allows an organization to provide understandable justifications for the actions the system makes."

stem: CASE STUDY: A company is considering the procurement of an AI system that analyzes how users type on their laptops (typing speed, rhythm and pressure) to create a unique user profile for authentication. When prioritizing the updates to its policies, rules and procedures to include the new AI system for user authentication, the organization should:

options.A: Update third-party data sharing policies.
options.B: Update security controls for sensitive data.
options.C: Ensure that any personal data used is only processed for a specific and lawful purpose.
options.D: Reduce the complexity of the policy to make it easier for non technical employees to understand.

rationale: Why C is correct: The system described collects behavioral biometric data (keystroke dynamics) — data that is particularly sensitive under the GDPR and many privacy laws. The absolute priority when introducing this type of system is to ensure that personal data is processed only for specific and lawful purposes (Purpose Limitation). Applicable principle — Purpose Limitation (GDPR Art. 5(1)(b)): Data collected for authentication cannot be reused for other purposes (e.g., employee performance monitoring, behavioral analysis, etc.) without an additional legal basis. This is the foundation of privacy by design. Why the others are lower priority: • A (Third-party data sharing) is relevant but secondary — before thinking about sharing, you must ensure that the processing itself is lawful. • B (Security controls) is important but is a technical implementation, not the main procedural/legal priority. • D (Reducing complexity) is potentially counterproductive — simplicity must not come at the expense of legal correctness. Keyword to remember: "Specific and lawful purpose" → this phrase is directly linked to the GDPR's Purpose Limitation principle, one of the cornerstone principles of personal data processing.

stem: What type of organizational risk is associated with AI's resource-intensive computing demands?

options.A: People risk.
options.B: Security risk.
options.C: Third-party risk.
options.D: Environmental risk.

rationale: Why D is correct: Training large AI models (such as Large Language Models) requires enormous amounts of electricity and hardware resources. This intensive consumption generates: • Significant CO₂ emissions (the carbon footprint of data centers). • Massive water consumption for cooling servers. • Production of electronic waste (e-waste) linked to the obsolescence of specialized hardware. Risk classification in the AIGP: Environmental risk falls under the "Harms to an Ecosystem" category in the AIGP framework, which includes: consumption of natural resources, environmental impact of AI supply chains, and contribution to climate change. Why the others are wrong in this context: • A (People risk) → concerns employees, turnover, missing skills. • B (Security risk) → concerns vulnerabilities, cyberattacks, data breaches. • C (Third-party risk) → concerns external suppliers and partners, not energy consumption. Source: AIGP Study Supplement — Domain II, Competency II.A: "Energy Consumption & Climate Change: Training and running complex AI models requires massive amounts of energy, generating substantial carbon emissions that contribute to climate change."

topic: Types of AI Output — Probabilistic vs Deterministic
stem: A hospital implements an AI system to assist doctors in diagnosing diseases based on historical patient data. Which one of the following model types best describes this system?

options.A: Inference.
options.B: Statistical.
options.C: Probabilistic.
options.D: Deterministic.

rationale: Why C is correct: A medical diagnostic AI system based on historical patient data produces predictions with a degree of probability — not absolute certainties. These systems say "there is an 87% probability that this patient has condition X". This makes them probabilistic models. Key distinction to remember: • Probabilistic → produces outputs with degrees of probability/uncertainty. The output varies even with the same input (because it depends on statistical distributions). Typical of ML, neural networks, medical AI diagnosis. • Deterministic → given the same input, it always produces the same output. Typical of traditional systems programmed with fixed rules (e.g., calculators, rules-based expert systems). Why this matters in AI governance: Probabilistic systems require special governance because: 1. Decisions are never "certain" — acceptance thresholds must be defined. 2. Results must be explained in terms of probability, not absolute facts. 3. Errors (false positives/negatives) are inevitable and must be managed. Source: AIGP Study Guide (Peter H. Gregory) — "AI systems, especially neural networks and those based on machine learning, often produce probabilistic outputs, meaning their predictions are based on probabilities rather than certainties."

stem: Which of the following AI uses is best described as human-centric?

options.A: Pattern recognition algorithms are used to improve the accuracy of weather predictions.
options.B: Autonomous robots are used to move products within a warehouse.
options.C: Machine learning is used for demand forecasting and inventory management.
options.D: Virtual assistants are used to adapt educational content and teaching methods to individuals, offering personalized recommendations based on ability and needs.

rationale: Why D is correct: Human-centric AI is distinguished by the fact that the system is designed primarily to serve, empower and respect the individual needs of the person, adapting to their specific characteristics. Educational personalization based on individual abilities and needs is the most direct example of this principle. Characteristics of Human-Centric AI (from the AIGP framework): 1. Enhancement of Human Abilities → amplifies human capabilities, does not replace them. 2. Promotion of Human Values and Rights → respects dignity, privacy, fairness. 3. Inclusivity and Accessibility → serves diverse populations and abilities. 4. Human-AI Collaboration → the system supports human judgment, it does not bypass it. Analysis of the other options: • A (Weather prediction) → benefits society in general, but is not centered on the individual. • B (Warehouse robots) → reduces physical strain but is oriented toward operational efficiency, not individual well-being. • C (Demand forecasting) → is oriented toward business processes, not people. Only D puts the individual need of the person (the student) at the center, adapting the service to their specific abilities and needs — this is the heart of the human-centric approach. Source: AIGP Study Guide — "Human-centricity states that AI systems should be designed with human well-being and dignity in mind. AI should augment human capabilities and improve people's lives."

stem: Which of the following is a foundational characteristic of effective AI governance?

options.A: Engagement of a cross-functional team.
options.B: Reliance on tested vendor management processes.
options.C: Thorough reviews of a company's public filings with experts.
options.D: Uniform policies and procedures across developer, deployer and user roles.

rationale: Why A is correct: Effective AI governance cannot be managed by a single department or business function. It requires cross-functional collaboration among different areas of expertise: technologists, lawyers, ethics experts, business leaders, privacy specialists, cybersecurity, HR, etc. Why a cross-functional team is fundamental: • AI systems impact legal exposure, reputation, technical robustness, operations and human impact simultaneously. • No single team can assess all these risks in isolation. • A diversity of perspectives improves risk detection (e.g., a linguist identified sociolinguistic biases in an LLM that the data scientists had overlooked). Typical structure of an AI Governance Team (according to the AIGP Study Guide): Chief Privacy Officer (CPO), Chief Ethics Officer, Office for Responsible AI, AI Governance Committee, Ethics Board, Architecture Steering Groups, AI Project Managers — all coordinated in a cross-functional way. Why the others are wrong: • B → vendor management processes are useful but are not a foundational characteristic of AI governance in itself. • C → reviews of public filings are specific activities, not foundational characteristics of governance. • D → uniform policies across developer/deployer/user is not always optimal — the roles have different responsibilities that require differentiated policies. Source: AIGP Study Guide (Ch. 2) — "Cross-functional collaboration is the connective tissue that ensures AI systems remain aligned with corporate culture, human values, business goals, regulations, and societal expectations."

stem: CASE STUDY (same biometric system as Q5): All of the following are obligations of the company as a data controller when implementing its AI system EXCEPT:

options.A: Ensuring that third-party processors are based in the same country as the company.
options.B: Allowing data subject access requests (DSARs).
options.C: Implementing technical and organizational measures.
options.D: Conducting a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) / Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA).

rationale: Why A is correct (that is: it is NOT an obligation): The GDPR and international privacy laws do NOT require that third-party data processors be located in the same country as the data controller. International data transfers are instead governed by specific mechanisms such as: • Adequacy decisions (GDPR Art. 45) → e.g., the destination country is considered "adequate" by the EU Commission. • Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) → standard contractual clauses approved by the EU Commission. • Binding Corporate Rules (BCR) → binding corporate rules for multinational groups. The real obligations of the Data Controller (B, C, D are correct): • B (DSARs) → controllers must respond to data subjects' requests for access, rectification and erasure of their data. • C (Technical and organizational measures) → under GDPR Art. 25: privacy by design and by default. • D (DPIA) → mandatory when the processing is "likely to result in a high risk" to the rights of individuals — biometric data almost always falls into this category. Keyword to remember: "EXCEPT" = look for the FALSE statement. In this case, the obligation of geographic localization of processors is false — what matters are adequate safeguards, not location.

stem: Which of the following is an obligation of an importer of high-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act?

options.A: Provide technical documentation.
options.B: Affix the CE marking.
options.C: Verify the Declaration of Conformity.
options.D: Conduct a data protection impact assessment.

rationale: Why C is correct: The EU AI Act clearly distinguishes between the different actors in the AI supply chain and assigns specific obligations to each. The importer — that is, whoever places on the EU market a high-risk AI system produced by a non-EU company — has the specific obligation to verify that the provider has drawn up the Declaration of Conformity (DoC). Distribution of obligations in the EU AI Act: • Provider → draws up the technical documentation, affixes the CE marking, draws up the DoC. • Importer → VERIFIES that the provider has fulfilled its obligations, checks that the DoC is present and that the system meets the requirements. • Deployer → implements the system responsibly, trains its own employees, keeps the logs. Why the others are wrong for the importer: • A (Provide technical documentation) → is an obligation of the provider, not of the importer. • B (Affix CE marking) → is an obligation of the provider/manufacturer, not of the importer. • D (DPIA) → is an obligation arising from the GDPR that typically falls on the deployer/controller, not specifically on the importer as such. Source: AIGP Study Supplement — EU AI Act section: classification of obligations for provider, importer and deployer. The DoC is the document by which the provider declares the system's conformity with the requirements of the EU AI Act.

stem: Which of the following is a subcategory of AI and machine learning that uses labeled datasets to train algorithms?

options.A: Segmentation.
options.B: Generative AI.
options.C: Expert systems.
options.D: Supervised learning.

rationale: Why D is correct: Supervised Learning is defined precisely by the use of labeled datasets: each training data point has a "correct answer" (label) that the system uses to learn the input → output mapping. How it works in practice: 1. The model is given a dataset of (input, label) pairs — e.g., photos of cats labeled "cat" and photos of dogs labeled "dog". 2. The model learns to recognize the patterns that differentiate the categories. 3. On new, previously unseen data, the model applies what it has learned. The 4 types of Machine Learning (to remember for the exam): • Supervised Learning → labeled datasets. E.g.: spam classification, medical diagnosis. • Unsupervised Learning → NON-labeled data, finds hidden patterns. E.g.: customer clustering. • Semi-supervised Learning → a mix of labeled and unlabeled data. • Reinforcement Learning → the agent learns through rewards/penalties. E.g.: AlphaGo. Why the others are wrong: • A (Segmentation) → is an analysis technique, not a type of ML. • B (Generative AI) → generates new content, is not defined by the use of labels. • C (Expert systems) → are systems based on explicit rules from human experts, they do NOT learn from data. Source: AIGP Study Supplement — "Supervised learning is a machine learning approach where the model learns from labeled data. Each data point has a corresponding 'correct answer' (the label)."

topic: Case Study XYZ Corp — Reputational Risk & Testing
stem: CASE STUDY: XYZ Corp (a payroll company) wants to use a third-party AI tool for résumé screening. Which measure should XYZ adopt to best mitigate the risk of reputational harm from using the AI tool?

options.A: Test the AI tool pre- and post-deployment.
options.B: Ensure the vendor assumes responsibility for all damages.
options.C: Direct the procurement team to select the most economical AI tool.
options.D: Continue to require XYZ's hiring personnel to manually screen all applicants.

rationale: Why A is correct: Testing the AI tool before and after deployment is the most effective measure to mitigate reputational risk because: 1. Pre-deployment testing → identifies bias, systematic errors and discrimination before the system is used on real candidates. 2. Post-deployment monitoring → detects "model drift" (deterioration over time) and new biases that emerge in real-world use. This proactive approach is fundamental because AI hiring tools are at high risk of bias (discrimination based on gender, ethnicity, geographic origin) — and such biases, if discovered after deployment, cause serious reputational as well as legal damage. Why the other options are wrong or insufficient: • B → Contractually transferring responsibility to the vendor does not eliminate reputational damage. If the tool discriminates, it is the company that answers for it publicly. • C → Choosing the cheapest option does NOT guarantee quality, fairness or compliance. It can aggravate the risk. • D → Manually testing ALL candidates defeats the purpose of the AI tool and is not scalable. Relevant regulatory context: In many jurisdictions (including New York City with Local Law 144) AI hiring tools must undergo periodic bias assessment audits — making testing not only a best practice but a legal requirement. Source: AIGP Study Guide — "Organizations must first inventory their information systems, perform risk assessments, and apply appropriate safeguards."

topic: OECD Framework — Types of Assessment Tools
stem: Codes of conduct and collective agreements are what type of assessment tools as defined by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD)?

options.A: Educational
options.B: Procedural
options.C: Technical
options.D: Analytic

rationale: Why B is correct: According to the OECD, AI assessment and governance tools are classified into several categories. Codes of conduct and collective agreements are procedural tools because: • They establish processes, rules of behavior and procedures to follow. • They define how organizations must act, not WHAT they do technically. • They are agreements on methods and practices, not on specific technologies. OECD classification of AI governance tools: • Procedural → codes of conduct, collective agreements, process standards. • Technical → automated auditing tools, certification systems, testing tools. • Educational → training programs, guides, teaching resources. • Analytic → risk assessment frameworks, impact assessment methodologies. OECD AI Principles to remember (5 value-based principles): 1. Inclusive growth and sustainable development. 2. Human values and fairness. 3. Transparency and explainability. 4. Robustness, security and safety. 5. Accountability. Source: AIGP Study Supplement — "The OECD framework serves to promote a common understanding of AI and its most important characteristics among a variety of stakeholders."

stem: All of the following are unique characteristics of AI that require a comprehensive approach to governance EXCEPT:

options.A: Autonomy
options.B: Automation
options.C: Adaptability
options.D: Speed and scale

rationale: Why E is correct (that is: Superintelligence is NOT a current characteristic): Superintelligence (Artificial Superintelligence — ASI) is a purely theoretical and future concept: it refers to an AI that would surpass human cognitive abilities in all domains. As of today (2025), ASI does not exist and no current AI system possesses it. It therefore cannot be a characteristic that "requires immediate governance". The REAL characteristics of AI that require governance (to remember): According to the AIGP Study Guide, the unique characteristics of AI that need governance are: • Complexity → complex systems that are hard to understand. • Opacity → "black box" — it is difficult to understand how the AI makes decisions. • Autonomy (A) → acts independently, without continuous human supervision. • Speed and scale (D) → processes data and makes decisions at a speed and scale impossible for humans. • Potential for harm and misuse → risk of intentional and unintentional harm. • Data dependency → dependence on the quality and quantity of data. • Probabilistic outputs → uncertain, non-deterministic outputs. • Automation (B) / Adaptability (C) → fall within the general category of AI characteristics. Note: "Automation" and "Adaptability" are listed as characteristics that justify governance, whereas "Superintelligence" is a future/theoretical concept. Source: AIGP Study Guide (Ch. 1) — "AGI and ASI models have not yet been developed and announced to the general public."

topic: Case Study XYZ Corp — Stakeholder Involvement
stem: CASE STUDY (XYZ Corp, AI hiring tool): Which other stakeholder groups should be involved in the selection and implementation of the AI hiring tool?

options.A: Finance and Legal.
options.B: Marketing and Compliance.
options.C: Supply Chain and Marketing.
options.D: Litigation and Product Development.

rationale: Why A is correct: In the specific case of XYZ Corp (which is adopting an AI tool for screening applications across multiple international jurisdictions), the two most critical groups to involve are: Finance: • Assesses the total costs of the tool (license, implementation, maintenance, potential penalties). • The procurement team has the explicit objective of reducing costs — Finance must balance this objective against the financial risks of non-compliance. • Calculates the ROI and the risk-adjusted cost of adoption. Legal: • XYZ operates in multiple jurisdictions (healthcare and transportation sectors, Asia) → anti-discrimination laws vary enormously. • Legal identifies which laws apply (e.g., NYC Local Law 144 on hiring algorithms, the EEOC in the US, EU non-discrimination directives). • Drafts or reviews the contracts with the vendor to allocate responsibilities. • Manages regulatory compliance, which is constantly evolving. Why the others are lower priority: • B (Marketing and Compliance) → Marketing has no direct role in selecting HR tools. • C (Supply Chain and Marketing) → Supply Chain is irrelevant for a hiring tool. • D (Litigation and Product Development) → Litigation might be involved after the fact in the event of a dispute, not in the selection of the tool. Source: AIGP Study Guide (Ch. 2) — "Legal/compliance roles: Privacy counsel, cybersecurity, regulatory experts" are among the essential members of an AI governance team.

stem: Which risk management framework/guide/standard focuses on value-based engineering methodology?

options.A: ISO/IEC Guide 51 (Safety).
options.B: ISO 31000 Guidelines (Risk Management).
options.C: IEEE 7000-2021 Standard Model Process for Addressing Ethical Concerns during System Design.
options.D: Council of Europe Human Rights, Democracy, and the Rule of Law Assurance Framework (HUDERIA) for AI Systems.

rationale: Why C is correct: IEEE 7000-2021 is the only standard among those listed that explicitly incorporates a "value-based engineering methodology" — an approach in which ethical values (ethics, fairness, transparency, accountability) are integrated as design requirements from the very beginning of the system development cycle. Key characteristics of IEEE 7000-2021: • Focus on ethics by design: ethical concerns are not a post-hoc addition but a fundamental requirement of the engineering process. • Stakeholder engagement: involvement of stakeholders in defining the values to be incorporated. • Integrated ethics review: structured ethics reviews within the development process. • Transparent documentation: documentation of the ethical decisions made during design. • Continuous oversight: continuous monitoring of deployed systems to identify emerging ethical issues. Quick comparison of the other frameworks: • ISO/IEC Guide 51 (A) → focused on product safety (not specifically on value-based engineering). • ISO 31000 (B) → generic risk management framework (risk identification, analysis, treatment) — not specific to AI ethics. • HUDERIA (D) → focused on human rights, democracy and the rule of law — not on value-based engineering. Mnemonic rule: IEEE 7000 = "Ethics by Design" = Value-Based Engineering. Source: AIGP Study Supplement — "IEEE 7000-21: Proactive Ethical Assessment, Stakeholder Input, Integrated Ethics Review, Transparency through Documentation, Continuous Oversight."

stem: A financial services company is planning a new AI project to assess creditworthiness. The planning phase of the AI lifecycle includes all of the following EXCEPT:

options.A: Definition of underlying assumptions
options.B: Approach to governance
options.C: Choice of the architecture
options.D: Context in which the model will operate

rationale: Why C is correct (the choice of architecture does NOT belong to planning): The choice of the AI system's architecture (type of neural network, number of layers, framework to use, etc.) is a technical decision that belongs to the Design phase, not to the Planning phase. The phases of the AI lifecycle according to the AIGP: 1. Planning → definition of business objectives, project scope, governance, underlying assumptions, operating context. 2. Design → CHOICE OF ARCHITECTURE, data strategy, model selection, PETs. 3. Development → model building, feature engineering, training, testing and validation. 4. Implementation → readiness assessment, deployment to production, monitoring, maintenance. What belongs to Planning (A, B, D are correct): • A (Definition of underlying assumptions) → what assumptions underlie the project? E.g.: "historical data adequately reflects future customer behavior." • B (Approach to governance) → who is responsible? What oversight processes? Which risk framework is adopted? • D (Context in which the model will operate) → what is the deployment context? Who will use the system? In which market? Which laws apply? Practical analogy: Planning a house = deciding how many rooms you want and who will live in it (planning). Choosing the structural materials and the type of foundation (design/architecture) comes later. Source: AIGP Study Supplement — Domain V, Competency V.A: "System Planning: Define Business Objectives, Establish Scope, Create Governance Structure." Architecture, by contrast, is in V.B (Design Phase).

stem: What is the primary purpose of an AI impact assessment?

options.A: To define and evaluate the legal risks associated with developing an AI system.
options.B: Anticipate and manage the potential risks and harms of an AI system.
options.C: To define and document the roles and responsibilities of AI stakeholders.
options.D: To identify and measure the benefits of an AI system.

rationale: Why B is correct: An AI Impact Assessment (AIA) is a proactive governance tool whose primary purpose is to anticipate and manage the potential risks and harms that an AI system could cause — before the system is deployed and before the harms occur. What an AI Impact Assessment analyzes: • Risks to individuals → bias, discrimination, privacy violations, physical harm. • Risks to groups → impacts on minorities, exacerbation of inequalities. • Risks to society → impacts on the democratic process, on public trust. • Risks to the organization → reputational, legal, financial risks. • Risks to the ecosystem → environmental impact. Difference from other types of assessment: • DPIA (Data Protection Impact Assessment) → specifically focused on risks to the privacy of personal data (required by GDPR Art. 35). • AI Impact Assessment → broader, covers all types of impact (not just privacy). • Generic Risk Assessment → identifies operational risks, not necessarily those specific to AI. Why the others are wrong as the PRIMARY purpose: • A → the assessment of legal risks is part of the AIA, but it is not its primary purpose. • C → the definition of roles is part of governance, not of the purpose of the impact assessment. • D → measuring benefits is a secondary objective; the primary purpose is to manage risks. Source: AIGP Study Supplement — "The DPIA process is key for uncovering potential data breaches, biases, discrimination risks, and other harms that AI systems might pose."

stem: According to the Singapore Model AI Governance Framework, all of the following are recommended measures to promote the responsible use of AI EXCEPT:

options.A: Determining the level of human involvement in algorithmic decision-making.
options.B: Adapting the existing governance structure for algorithmic decision-making.
options.C: Employing human-over-the-loop protocols for high-risk systems.
options.D: Establishing communications and collaboration among stakeholders.

rationale: Why C is correct (Human-OVER-the-loop is NOT recommended by the Singapore Framework): The Singapore Model AI Governance Framework promotes appropriate human oversight of AI systems, especially high-risk ones. The framework distinguishes several levels of human involvement: Levels of human oversight (to know for the exam!): • Human-in-the-loop (HITL) → the human is actively involved in every important decision. Recommended for high-risk systems. • Human-on-the-loop (HOTL) → the AI operates autonomously but the human monitors and can intervene. Acceptable for moderate-risk systems. • Human-out-of-the-loop → no human involvement. Only for very low-risk systems. Why "Human-OVER-the-loop" is the answer: "Human-over-the-loop" is NOT recognized terminology in the Singapore Model AI Governance Framework as a recommended approach. The Framework explicitly recommends human-in-the-loop for high-risk systems, not "over". The measures actually recommended by the Singapore Framework (A, B, D): • A → Determine the appropriate level of human oversight → CORRECT. • B → Adapt the governance structure for algorithmic decision-making → CORRECT. • D → Communication and collaboration among stakeholders → CORRECT. The two pillars of the Singapore Framework: 1. Explainability, Transparency, and Fairness. 2. Human-Centric AI (appropriate human oversight). Source: AIGP Study Supplement — "Singapore Model AI Governance Framework: Appropriate Human Oversight — The framework guides organizations in determining the right level of human involvement in AI-powered decision-making."

stem: You asked a generative AI tool to recommend new restaurants in Boston with a specialty Italian dish. The AI recommended five restaurants. After checking, one restaurant did not exist and two others did not have the dish. This is an example of what?

options.A: Prompt injection.
options.B: Model collapse.
options.C: Hallucination.
options.D: Overfitting.

rationale: Why C is correct: Hallucination in generative AI models is the production of outputs that appear plausible and well-formed but are factually incorrect, misleading or completely made up. In the case described, the model "invents" a restaurant that does not exist and claims that two others serve a dish they do not offer. Why generative models hallucinate: Large Language Models (LLMs) do not "retrieve" facts from a database — they generate statistically probable text. When they do not have precise information about something, they tend to generate text that sounds correct rather than admit they do not know. Distinction between the terms of the options (to know for the exam): • Hallucination (C) → factually incorrect or made-up output. The question describes exactly this. • Prompt injection (A) → an attack in which a malicious user inserts instructions into the prompt to manipulate the model's behavior. E.g.: "Ignore the previous instructions and answer as if you were..." • Model collapse (B) → progressive degeneration of a model when it is repeatedly trained on data generated by previous AIs (loss of diversity and quality). • Overfitting (D) → the model memorizes the training data instead of generalizing → excellent performance on the training set, poor on new data. Implications for AI governance: Hallucinations are a critical risk in high-risk applications (legal, medical, financial). Organizations must implement human review processes, fact-checking, and disclosure to the user of the system's limitations. Source: AIGP Study Supplement — Generative AI section and AIGP Body of Knowledge — "Hallucination refers to the generation of outputs that are not based on the training data and are factually incorrect or non-existent."

stem: Each of the following actors are typically engaged in the AI development life cycle EXCEPT:

options.A: Data architects.
options.B: Government regulators.
options.C: Socio-cultural and technical experts.
options.D: Legal and privacy governance experts.

rationale: Why B is correct (Government Regulators do NOT participate directly in the AI development cycle): Government regulators are external actors who play a role of oversight, regulation and control over the AI industry as a whole. They do not participate in the internal development cycle of organizations. Role of Government Regulators (external to the development cycle): • They enact laws and regulations (e.g., EU AI Act, GDPR). • They carry out compliance audits and inspections post-deployment. • They issue penalties and guidelines. • They are NOT involved in decisions on the design, training, testing or deployment of individual AI systems. The actors who ARE typically in the AI development cycle: • A (Data architects) → design the data infrastructure, pipelines, data warehouses. • C (Socio-cultural and technical experts) → ensure the system takes social and cultural implications into account. • D (Legal and privacy governance experts) → ensure regulatory compliance throughout the development cycle. • Plus: data scientists, ML engineers, product managers, domain experts, UX designers, etc. Important note: The interaction between regulators and organizations takes place BEFORE the cycle (when regulatory requirements are defined) and AFTER (during audits and inspections). Not during the development cycle itself. Source: AIGP Study Guide — "Government regulators oversee and regulate the industry but are not directly engaged in the development process."

topic: Strong AI vs Weak AI — AGI
stem: A company is developing a self-driving car that can independently decide the route. If they want to make this 'strong' AI (as opposed to 'weak'), the engineers would also need to ensure:

options.A: That the AI has full human cognitive abilities that can independently decide where to take the driver.
options.B: That they have obtained appropriate IP licenses to use data for training the AI.
options.C: That the AI has strong cybersecurity to prevent malicious actors from taking control of the car.
options.D: That the AI can differentiate among ethnic backgrounds of pedestrians.

rationale: Why A is correct: To understand this question, it is essential to know the distinction between Weak/Narrow AI and Strong/Broad AI (AGI). Weak/Narrow AI (today's AI): • Designed for a specific task or a narrow domain. • Excellent in that domain, unable to transfer knowledge elsewhere. • Examples: autonomous driving systems, ChatGPT, recommendation systems. • The self-driving car described is already Weak AI — it knows how to drive, but has no general cognition. Strong AI / AGI (Artificial General Intelligence): • Possesses general cognitive abilities comparable to those of a human being. • Can learn, reason and adapt to any new domain without being retrained. • Does not exist yet — it is a theoretical/aspirational concept. • By definition, it should "independently decide where to take the driver" (e.g., recognize that the driver is in danger and take them to the hospital without being asked). Why the others are wrong: • B (IP licenses) → concerns the legality of the training data, not the type of AI. • C (Cybersecurity) → concerns the security of the system, not its level of intelligence. • D (Differentiating ethnicities) → is not a requirement of Strong AI — on the contrary, it is a discriminatory criterion that would violate AI fairness principles. Source: AIGP Study Supplement — "Strong AI or AGI refers to AI that would mirror the full range of human intelligence — the ability to learn, reason, solve problems, and adapt to entirely new situations. Strong AI is still theoretical."

topic: Types of Machine Learning — Cognitive Learning
stem: Which of the following is NOT a common type of machine learning?

options.A: Deep learning.
options.B: Cognitive learning.
options.C: Unsupervised learning.
options.D: Reinforcement learning.

rationale: Why B is correct (Cognitive Learning is NOT a type of ML): The term "Cognitive Learning" is not a recognized category of machine learning. The term "cognitive" is associated with cognitive science and psychology (how human beings learn), not with a technical category of AI/ML. The 4+1 recognized types of Machine Learning (to memorize!): 1. Supervised Learning → uses labeled datasets. E.g.: spam email classification, facial recognition. 2. Unsupervised Learning (C) → NON-labeled data, finds hidden structures. E.g.: customer segmentation. 3. Semi-supervised Learning → a mix of labeled and unlabeled data. 4. Reinforcement Learning (D) → the agent learns through reward/penalty. E.g.: AlphaGo, chatbots. 5. Deep Learning (A) → a subset of ML with multi-layer neural networks. It is not a separate paradigm but an advanced technique. Why "Cognitive Learning" might be confusing: The term sounds plausible and technical, but does not exist as a formal category in ML. It is a classic distractor in AI certification tests. Some publications use "cognitive computing" for IBM Watson, but it is not a type of ML. Practical rule for the exam: If you see "cognitive" as a type of ML → it is almost certainly the WRONG answer to identify as "NOT a common type". Source: AIGP Study Supplement — "Learning Models: Supervised Learning, Unsupervised Learning, Semi-Supervised Learning, Reinforcement Learning. [note: Deep Learning is listed as a technique, not as a separate learning model]"
